gloss: “This is the morning of the day after Satan’s coming to the earth” (Todd). *clime*, region.
the “leaves.” The wind which ushers in the dawn stirs the leaves as a fan, and their rustling helps to awake Adam.
i.e. mild as the west wind passing over a bank of flowers. Flora, the goddess of flowers, symbolises the flower-world. Her association with Zephyrus is a poetic convention.
i.e. balm (= balsam, etymologically). *drops*; myrrh and balm are aromatic resins, of much the same nature, produced by the balsam-tree and other trees of the same genus.
Explained by IV. 799 et seq. The abruptness of the sentences expresses Eve’s confusion on just awakening, and her agitation of mind.

i.e. the nightingale; the poet’s favourite bird, as many allusions show. No doubt, the garden of his father’s house at Horton was a haunt of the bird. *his*; poetic tradition (due to the classical story of Philomela) would say *her*, but the male bird is the songster.
Contrast IV. 657 et seq., where Eve asks wherefore, for whom, do the stars shine all night, to which Adam replies that there are “millions of spiritual creatures” on earth, unseen by men.
It is implied that the figure which appeared was that of Satan; cf. III. 636–44 where, to deceive Uriel, he puts on the form of a Cherub, winged and with flowing locks—as here. *Ambrosia*, fragrance.
i.e. is it envy or some reservation, restraint, that keeps you from being tasted?
Satan speaks as “prince of air” (XII. 454). In *P. R.* I. 39–46 he addresses his followers as “ancient powers of air.” The idea can be traced to Ephesians ii. 2.

For Milton “Fancy” is the loftiest form of imagination; cf. VIII. 461, where he terms it “internal sight,” i.e. the highest power of conceiving mentally that which is not present to the eye. *represent*, i.e. present, give representations of.
dawn, daybreak. Cf. Luke i. 78, “the day-spring from on high.”

We must observe the strong emphasis on “unmeditated,” and the repetition of “various” in 146—unmistakeable hints at the poet’s “preference of extemporary prayer over set forms” (Keightley). In *Eikonoklastes* he sneers at the use of a “service-book.”
The hymn is obviously based upon Psalm cxlviii. and the Canticle, “O all ye Works of the Lord.”
“that is, without such night as ours, for the darkness there is no more than ‘grateful twilight’” (Newton). *symphonies*, harmonies.

He refers to the planet Venus, which, when west of the sun, rises and sets before him, and is called the Morning-star, Lucifer; when the planet is east of the sun, it rises and sets after him, and is called the Evening-star, Hesperus.

i.e. the planets. He has already mentioned the Sun, Moon (then reckoned planets) and Venus: hence only four planets remain—Mercury, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. Possibly M. by a mere error said *five* instead of *four*; but I think that he intended to include Venus again.

*not without*; Lat. *non sine*. M. is fond of this classical turn of phrase. *song*, i.e. “the music of the spheres.” According to tradition, Pythagoras was the only man who ever heard this music. Here, before the Fall, Adam and Eve possess the power which through their sin humanity lost.
Editors think that M. had in mind that celebrated prayer in Plato: “O Jupiter, give us good things, whether we pray for them or not, and remove from us all evil things even though we pray for them.”
alluding to the pretty classical fancy of the vine being wedded to (because trained to grow up) the elm; cf. Horace, *Odes* IV. 5. 30.

There is the same allusion in IV. 167–71 to the story of Tobias and his victory over Asmodeus (one of the evil angels) as told in the Apocryphal Book of Tobit. The name means ‘divine healer,’ or ‘health of God.’
Cf. the well-known passage in I. 287–91. Galileo died in 1642; “glass of Galileo” is only a general term for the instrument associated with his name.
Strictly, Delos was, and Samos was not, one of the circular group of islands in the Ægean called Cyclades.
The metaphor is that of separating grain from the chaff. *winnows*, parts, cleaves. For *buxom* = ‘yielding,’ see the note on II. 842.

Most accounts describe the Phoenix as a solitary bird, living “in the Arabian woods” for 500 years. Only one Phoenix lived at a time. *gazed by all*, i.e. gazed on. *Egyptian Thebes*, the famous city of that name in Upper Egypt, which he calls “Egyptian” to distinguish it from the Bœotian town.

Suggested, obviously, by Isaiah vi. 2: “each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly.” *lineaments*, his limbs generally; not merely the features of his face.
Hermes (or Mercury), son of Zeus and Maia—the winged messenger of the gods. The point of the simile lies in the fact that Mercury was typical of grace and beauty.

The plants are often mentioned together—no doubt, from their association in Scripture. The cassia spoken of in the Bible was a spice of the nature of cinnamon. The nard or spikenard of Scripture was a fragrant Indian root.

lemma: as in the door he sat
gloss: “And the Lord appeared unto him in the plains of Mamre: and he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day,” Genesis xviii. 1. The whole chapter is in Milton’s thoughts here where he describes Adam’s entertainment of Raphael.
The name Adam is said to signify ‘red earth.’ *inspired*, i.e. filled with “the breath of life” (Gen. ii. 7).

He supposes the garden of Eden to produce the fruits for which in after-times different parts of the world were famous; and, as usual, he selects places round the names of which cluster literary (especially classical) associations.

lemma: In Pontus, or the Punic coast
gloss: Pontus, in the N.E. region of Asia Minor, on the coast of the Euxine or Black Sea, was noted for its fruit and nut trees. *Punic coast*, i.e. Africa, more particularly Carthage.
Alcinous was the king of the Phaeacians, a fabulous race whom Homer places in the island of Scheria. He entertained Odysseus, and Homer describes his palace and gardens at length.
*inoffensive*, not intoxicating, as it became through “the later invention of fermenting the juice of the grape” (Thyer). *must*, new wine; Lat. *mustum*. *meaths*, sweet beverages.
One of those passing touches in which M. reveals his republicanism and dislike of ostentation.
The word must not be pressed, as in *P. L.* Raphael is an archangel.

Alluding to the *judicium Paridis*. The three goddesses, Hera, Athena and Aphrodite, each claimed the golden apple inscribed with the words “to the fairest.” The matter was referred to the shepherd Paris, who decided in favour of Aphrodite. *Ida*, the “many-fountained” mountain in Mysia, Asia Minor.
“And the angel came in unto her, and said, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee,” Luke i. 28. *second Eve*; so Christ is “the last Adam,” 1 Cor. xv. 45.
i.e. the different charms of spring and autumn (as we know them) were then united in one continuous season.
M. regards the spots in the moon as vapours not entirely assimilated to her substance, and therefore visible against their luminous background.
i.e. the angel did actually eat—not merely appear to eat, as theologians explain in such cases. *gloss*, interpretation.

“as by means of the heat produced by coal, the alchemist can drive off the grosser particles and leave the pure gold remaining; so the internal heat of the angelic body drives off through the pores the innutritious particles of the food” (Keightley). *empiric*, experimentising.
The phrase (from Gen. vi. 2) has been taken to mean either the angels or the pious descendants of Seth. Here M. apparently adopts the former view.

His views, as admirably summarised by Dr Masson, amount to this—“that all created Being, whether called soul or body, consists of but one primordial matter, differentiated into an ascending series of forms, from the inorganic as the lowest, up to the vegetable, thence to the animal, thence to the human, and so to the angelic.”
*scale*, ladder, Lat. *scala*. *sublimed*, raised; the metaphor is probably from the science of chemistry, in which to *sublime* is to ‘raise or elevate by heat.’

intuition, as its derivation (Lat. *intueri*, ‘to look into’) implies, being the faculty of seeing into things straightway and apprehending truth without any process of reasoning: discourse, the lower faculty of understanding things by means of reasoning processes.

“Matter” (472) is the “centre,” and “Nature” the “scale” which reaches to the utmost of our conceptions, all round. By ascending this ladder, i.e. by the study of Nature, we are led to God (Richardson).
Cf. *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 3, “in assigning the gift of free will, God suffered both men and angels to stand or fall at their own uncontrolled choice.”
i.e. since he has laid on us only one command, whereas he might have imposed many, we ought to feel bound to obey that command, even if it were not “just,” as it is.

We may compare the long episodical description that follows of the expulsion of the apostate angels from Heaven with Æneas’ narrative to Dido of the fall of Troy. Raphael is briefer; his narrative closes at 892 of bk. VI.

lemma: what if Earth … Be but the shadow of Heaven
gloss: M. hints that after all earth may be but a symbol of Heaven—an idea which under various forms has occurred to many thinkers.

He has borrowed Plato’s conception of the *Annus Magnus*. This was the vast period at the close of which the heavenly spheres, having completed their several revolutions, come back to the position whence they started.

Upon the peculiar theological bearing of this passage it is unnecessary to comment; we have already seen Milton’s Arianism. Many texts of Scripture are alluded to here. Cf. Ps. ii. 6, 7 (“Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee”).
Alluding again to the music of the spheres. He compares the rhythmic movements of the angels to the revolutions (“wheels”) of the planets and fixed stars.
We hear of “angels’ food,” Psalm lxxviii. 25. *rubied* = ‘red as rubies.’
The “high mount of God” is what M. in *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 7, calls “the highest heaven, as it were the supreme citadel and habitation of God.”

*pavilions*, tents = tabernacles (from Lat. *tabernaculum*, a dimin. of *taberna*, ‘a shed or hut’). *Tabernaculum* is used in the Vulgate of the tent that sheltered the Ark, whence it passed into the Authorised Version.
what this was we are not told, because, as M. says in I. 361–63, the names which the apostate angels had before their fall were “blotted out and razed,” so that there might be no memorial of them.

lemma: Homeward … The quarters of the North
gloss: Commonly Lucifer was made monarch of the north—in allusion to Isai. xiv. 12, 13, “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north.”
Alluding to Satan’s subsequent title Lucifer—‘day-star.’

lemma: Innumerable as the stars of night
gloss: “What an imagination the old man had! Milton beats everyone in the material sublime” (Tennyson). Wordsworth uses *impearl* similarly of dew in *To the Daisy*.
aiming at, seeking to obtain; cf. Lat. *affectare*.
Satan addresses the angels by their habitual titles, and then sarcastically adds that he is not quite sure whether they ought still to claim those titles.

i.e. if I may be sure that I know you aright, or if you know yourselves to be—as you are—sons of Heaven. *possessed*; implying that formerly “Heaven” was equally enjoyed by all its inhabitants, but now has been usurped by the Almighty as His alone.
i.e. who, as it is, without the restraint of any law, avoid sin. Why, he contends, impose laws on those who need no law to make them walk aright?
having no successor, i.e. everlasting.
The argument seems to be that Christ, by becoming the head of the angels, became in a measure one of them, and so ennobled their nature.
Contrast IV. 42, 43, where Satan admits (to himself) what he here denies, viz. that he and the other angels were created by God.
the course of fate. “Our author makes Satan a sort of fatalist. No compliment to fatalism to put it into the mouth of the Devil” (Newton).
another of those jingles which M. uses generally to express sarcasm or contempt—as here.

Cf. Numbers xvi. 26, “Depart, I pray you, from the tents of these wicked men”—an appropriate allusion, as Moses is there dissuading the congregation of Israel from joining Korah and his followers who, like Satan and his angels, were rebels. *devoted*, doomed.
A favourite type of verse with M. Perhaps, when he wrote this line Milton had in mind his own position at the Restoration. The personal note is strong in his poetry.
